blocks.text: What an AI assistant for instructional designers does on a Mac

An AI assistant for instructional designers should help with the work around the course, not only the course itself. Lazur covers the everyday parts. It explains what is on your screen, points at menus, dictates text and drafts first versions. It also keeps reminders and calendar events moving while you work.

Lazur lives in the notch of your Mac. You hold ⌥⌘ and ask. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the keys, then answers out loud. It is not a plugin or add-in, so it does not sit inside Articulate or PowerPoint as a feature. It works next to them.

It also does not click for you. Ask where something is and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. You keep your hands on the work.

items: Explain: reads what is open and answers your questions about it out loud.
Point: circles the menu or button you cannot find.
Dictate: hold fn to type clean, formatted text at the cursor.
Draft and research: writes a first version into your doc, and summarizes sources in its own Chrome tabs.

blocks.text: Where an instructional designer's time goes

Nobody has measured how instructional designers split their computer time by task or app. The closest official source is the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics page for training and development specialists. That page lists duties but gives no time shares. Treat any ranking of tasks as a guide, not a measurement.

The BLS duty list covers a lot of ground. Specialists assess training needs through surveys, interviews and consultations. They design manuals, online modules and course materials. They review materials, deliver training, help evaluate programs, and handle admin such as monitoring costs and scheduling classes. BLS also says much of the work involves people, presentations and leading training. Not all of it happens at a keyboard.
Instructional design duties mapped to Lazur's help

rows: Assess training needs with surveys and interviews
Explain open survey results and summarize interview notes out loud
Design manuals, modules and course materials

blocks.text: Read the middle column as your own map. Your team may use a different survey tool or authoring platform. The right column shows where Lazur saves a few steps. It does not replace the job. Lazur answers questions about your screen. It does not decide what a learner needs to know.
Working through a real day with Lazur

A typical day mixes short tasks with long blocks of writing. Start by clearing the small things by voice. Ask Lazur to summarize the overnight SME emails, set a reminder and add the review call to Calendar. Those take seconds. They keep the inbox from taking over the morning.

Save the longer work for the middle of the day. Dictate your first draft of the learner survey, then ask Lazur for question drafts. Check each question against the approved procedure. Lazur writes fast, but it knows your policy only if you tell it or show it on screen.

End with admin and research. Ask for a summary of how other teams score scenario quizzes, then decide what goes into the course. Keep a short list of open questions for the SME. Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked and did on the Mac, so you can find it later.
Dictating course text at the cursor

Hold fn and speak. Lazur types clean, formatted text where your cursor sits, in any app. That works in Google Docs for scripts, in PowerPoint for speaker notes and in a survey tool for item wording. It is a plain, fast way to get a first draft out of your head. You can test how well your own speech comes through with the [dictation accuracy checker](/tools/dictation-accuracy-checker).

Set up the personal dictionary before your first long session. Add course names, product codes, acronyms and the SME's name spelling. Use snippets for text you type every week, such as a standard course disclaimer or your team's learning objective format. Clipboard slots hold reusable blocks, such as a rubric paragraph.

items: Dictating a whole module in one breath. Speak in short sentences and check each paragraph.
Skipping the personal dictionary. Product names and acronyms come out wrong, and you fix them later.
Pasting dictated text without reading it. A mis-heard number, step or warning can reach learners.
Keeping an old snippet after a policy changes. Update snippets when your procedures change.

blocks.text: Reviewing SME drafts in Google Docs

SME drafts often arrive with solid facts and rough structure. You need their content and your order. Google Docs lets you suggest edits, so the SME can accept or reject each one. Lazur helps you find the setting. You make the change yourself.

Switch the editing mode to Suggesting before you touch the text. In Google Docs, the mode menu sits near the Share button at the top right of the window. Once it is set, your changes show as suggestions. For one edit or all of them at once, read [how to accept or reject suggestions in Google Docs](/how-to/accept-or-reject-suggestions-in-google-docs). More on the workflow is on the [Google Docs page for instructional designers](/for/instructional-designers/google-docs).

blocks.title: Ask where, then do it
blocks.text: Hold ⌥⌘ and ask where a setting lives. Lazur circles it, then you click. That is faster than hunting through menus, and you keep control of every change.
Building storyboards and templates in PowerPoint

Many storyboards start as a deck. Each slide holds one screen of the learner's path. Put the on-screen text in the body and the narration in the notes. Set the layout once in the Slide Master, so every slide inherits it. Open it from View > Slide Master.

Ask Lazur to guide you through the master. It gives one step, then waits for your click. Change the title font once in the master, and every slide follows. Keep the master simple. A master with many layouts is hard for the next designer to use.

Dictate narration into the notes at the cursor, then ask Lazur to draft short on-screen text. Check each line against your storyboard. For more on this workflow, see the [PowerPoint page for instructional designers](/for/instructional-designers/powerpoint).
Articulate Storyline and Rise on a Mac

Storyline 360 is the one that trips up Mac users. Parallels says Storyline 360 is Windows-exclusive. On a Mac it runs only in a virtual machine, and Apple silicon Macs need a Windows 11 Pro or Enterprise (Arm) VM. You also need a Windows license and Articulate 360 licenses.

Lazur sees what is on your Mac screen. A virtual machine window is part of that screen, but whether Lazur reads a Windows app inside one is something to test. Run a short check with a simple question before you rely on it during a real build.

Rise is a different case. Articulate describes Rise as web-based course authoring, so you work in a browser. Parallels says Rise 360 and Review 360 run natively on a Mac. Either way, Lazur can point at buttons in the browser window you already have open.

blocks.title: Check the requirements first
blocks.text: Vendor pages change. Confirm the current Mac requirements on Articulate's support site before you buy a license or set up a virtual machine.
Research for course content and checking sources
Ask Lazur to research a topic and it works in its own Chrome tabs. It comes back with a summary and a report. Good research starts with the source, so open the links and read each claim in context.

Here is a real example. The 28% email figure appears in many articles. It comes from a 2012 McKinsey report on interaction workers, and a secondary article cites it. The sample and method were not checked. Quote it as a 2012 estimate for interaction workers, not as a measure of instructional designers.
Save the source list next to your draft. A summary is a starting point for your own reading. It is not a citation for a course, and your reviewers will ask where each fact came from.
Privacy and your employer's rules for course data

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer your question. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Read Lazur's privacy statement before you rely on those terms.

Instructional designers often handle employee records, client content and learner data. Your employer sets the rules for that data, and Lazur does not change them. This page makes no compliance claims for Lazur. Check your own company's policy before you share anything on screen with an AI tool.

items: Check whether the draft contains learner records, health details or client names.
Close or hide those windows before you hold the keys.
Ask your manager or IT team which AI tools are allowed for course content.
Keep dictated notes that hold personal details out of shared docs.

blocks.text: Mistakes people make with an AI assistant for course design

items: Treating the first draft as final. Read every question and check it against the approved source.
Asking vague questions. Name the app and the goal, such as where suggesting mode is in Google Docs.
Leaving private data on screen. Close the window before you ask about the screen.
Expecting Lazur to click. It points and guides. You do the clicking.
Skipping the test run. Try one small task on a copy of a real file before a big build.

blocks.text: What to do next with Lazur

Start with one repeat task. Pick something you do every week, such as drafting knowledge checks or setting up a master. Try it on a copy of the course, not the live file. The guide to [making a copy of a document in Google Docs](/how-to/make-a-copy-of-a-document-in-google-docs) shows the steps.

Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. Download the app from the [download page](/download). The free trial starts when you first open the app, and it needs no credit card. Compare plans on the [pricing page](/pricing).

faq.question: Is there an AI assistant made specifically for instructional designers?
faq.answer: Not as a plugin for one authoring tool. Lazur is a general voice assistant for the Mac that works in any app, including Google Docs and PowerPoint. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it does not operate other apps for you.

faq.question: Does Lazur work with Articulate Storyline on a Mac?
faq.answer: Parallels says Storyline 360 is Windows-exclusive and runs on a Mac only in a Windows virtual machine. Lazur sees what your Mac screen shows, so you need to test it inside your own VM setup. Do not assume it works there until you have tried it on a simple question.

faq.question: Will Lazur click buttons in my course files?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points, explains and guides. In guide mode it waits for each click, and you press the button. It can draft and type text and dictate at the cursor. You make the edits and the final choices.

faq.question: Can I paste learner records or client data into it?
faq.answer: Check your employer's rules first. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Content is not used to train AI models. Your employer's policy still decides what you may share.

faq.question: Is Lazur available on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available.

faq.question: How do I try it without a credit card?
faq.answer: Download the app from the download page. The free trial starts when you first open the app, and it needs no credit card. Compare plans on the pricing page before you choose one.

faq.question: Does this replace an instructional designer?
faq.answer: No. The duties BLS lists, from needs analysis to evaluation, depend on judgment about learners and goals. Lazur takes some routine work off your plate, such as drafting options, setting reminders and finding menu settings.

painPoints.title: Email takes a large share of the week
painPoints.text: A 2012 McKinsey estimate put email at 28% of the workweek for interaction workers. No study measures instructional designers alone, but review threads and scheduling land in the inbox all day.

painPoints.title: Needs analysis is slow to write up
painPoints.text: BLS lists surveys, interviews and consultations as the first step. The notes from them still have to become a plan, and that writing takes real time.

painPoints.title: Reviewing SME drafts is messy
painPoints.text: SMEs send content in email, chat and Word files. You merge their facts with your structure, check accuracy and track which edits were accepted.

painPoints.title: The blank page for quiz questions
painPoints.text: Writing knowledge checks, feedback and scenarios from scratch is slow. The first draft is often the hardest part of a module.

painPoints.title: Admin keeps interrupting the design
painPoints.text: BLS lists monitoring costs and scheduling classes as typical duties. These small tasks break up design time and are easy to forget.

painPoints.title: Authoring tools do not all run on a Mac
painPoints.text: Storyline 360 is Windows-exclusive. On a Mac you need a virtual machine, a Windows license and Articulate 360 licenses, according to Parallels.
